narr: Let's dive into some key concepts in C programming, focusing on stock management, control flow, and input-output operations.
We'll start by examining how we can check if we have enough resources to make a coffee drink.

data.heading: Checking Coffee Ingredients
data.code:
return stock.water_ml >= recipe.water_ml &&
stock.milk_ml >= recipe.milk_ml &&
stock.beans_g >= recipe.beans_g &&
stock.paper_cups >= recipe.paper_cups;

narr: This function checks if we have enough ingredients to make a specific coffee drink.
It returns true only if all four conditions are met: water, milk, beans, and paper cups.

We have no paper cups, so the result is false, even though other ingredients are sufficient.
Here's a summary of our stock testing results.
The first two cases have all required ingredients, while the third lacks paper cups.

data.heading: Updating Stock After Coffee

narr: Now let's see how we update our stock after making coffee.
This function first checks if we can make the coffee.
If yes, it subtracts all four ingredients from the stock.
Then it returns the updated stock.

data.heading: Stock Update Comparison
data.problem: Compare two different calls to stock_after_coffee
steps: Result: returned copy is discarded, original stock unchanged
Result: returned copy is saved to stock variable
data.result: Only the second call actually updates the stock

narr: There's an important difference between these two function calls.
The first call creates a new copy of stock but doesn't save it.
The second call saves the returned copy back to the stock variable.
Only the second approach actually updates our stock levels.
Here's what happens to our stock when we properly save the result.
We see the water decreased by 100ml, milk by 50ml, beans by 10g, and cups by 1.

data.heading: Order Processing Block

narr: This is a complete order processing block.
First, we print the current stock.
Then we check if we can make the coffee.
If yes, we update stock and create a cup record.
Finally, we print the updated stock and cup information.

data.title: Control Flow
data.subtitle: goto, spaghetti code and error handling

narr: Now let's discuss control flow in C, particularly the controversial goto statement.
While generally discouraged, goto has some legitimate uses in C programming.

data.heading: goto Statement Example

narr: The goto statement allows unconditional jumps to any labeled point in the same function.
Here, if the condition is true, the code jumps to the 'outside' label.
Otherwise, it executes some code and then returns to the 'start' label.
Edsger Dijkstra famously argued that excessive use of goto creates 'spaghetti code'.
This makes code harder to read and debug.
Fortunately, any code using goto can be rewritten without it.

data.heading: goto in C
bullets: Can be replaced with structured control flow
Has one legitimate use: exiting nested blocks
In C++, Java, etc., exceptions handle error recovery
In C, goto provides a clean way to jump to error handling

narr: Despite Dijkstra's criticism, goto has one legitimate use in C.
In languages with exception handling like C++ and Java, errors are handled through exceptions.
But in C, which lacks exceptions, goto provides a clean way to exit nested blocks and handle errors.
This pattern allows jumping to an 'error:' label, skipping multiple levels of nested code.

data.title: Input-Output
data.subtitle: putchar/getchar, printf and its formats, scanf

narr: Let's now explore input-output operations in C.
These are provided by the standard library <stdio.h>, not the language itself.
There are two types of streams: text streams and binary streams.

data.heading: Stream Types
bullets: Text stream: series of strings ending with '\n'
Binary stream: series of raw bytes
Library streams are buffered for efficiency

narr: In C, we work with streams, which can be text or binary.
Text streams consist of strings ending with newline characters.
The library handles platform-specific line endings automatically.
Binary streams contain raw bytes without any interpretation.
Both types use buffering to improve performance.

data.heading: Character Input-Output Example

narr: This example demonstrates basic character input and output.
getchar() reads a character from standard input.
putchar() writes a character to standard output.
The program converts uppercase letters to lowercase.
It continues until end of file (EOF) is encountered.
To read from a file instead of standard input, we use the '<' operator.
This is an OS feature, not a language feature.
The shell redirects file input to our program's stdin.

data.heading: printf Function
bullets: Formatted output: printf(char format[], arg1, arg2, ...)
Format contains literal text and specifiers starting with %

narr: The printf function provides formatted output.
It takes a format string followed by any number of arguments.
It returns the number of characters it printed.
The format string contains both literal text and conversion specifiers.
Each specifier starts with % and can include flags, width, precision, and length modifiers.
printf supports various type specifiers for different data types.
For integers, we have d/i for decimal, u for unsigned, and x/X for hexadecimal.
For characters and strings, we use c and s respectively.
For floating point, we have f for standard format and e/E for exponential notation.
To print a literal percent sign, we use %% in the format string.

data.heading: Length Modifiers
rows: interpret as short; use with i, d, o, u, x
interpret as long; use with i, d, o, u, x
interpret as double; use with e, f, g

narr: Length modifiers change how printf interprets the argument.
h specifies a short integer, l specifies a long integer,
and L specifies a long double for floating-point values.

data.heading: printf Width Formatting
data.result:
%4d prints '  10' (2 spaces before 10)
%7s prints '   hello' (2 spaces before hello)

narr: Width formatting allows us to specify minimum field width.
For example, %4d ensures the integer takes at least 4 characters, padding with spaces if needed.
Similarly, %7s ensures the string takes at least 7 characters.
